overview: **AGI by 2028** produces the highest average worry, 3.54, compared with 1.76 in AI Plateau across these 206 interviews.
**More warning** increases opportunities to prepare, while present bills, lost hours and unconfirmed future income continue to shape private concerns.
**Money cushions** separate responses throughout: thin-cushion worry averages 2.85 in AGI by 2036, compared with 1.79 for strong cushions.

S0.headline: Most carry on, but unchanged technology leaves ordinary household and job insecurity intact.

whatTheyDo.text: **200 of 206** carry on, from supervised wiring with checks to experienced repairs and familiar records.
**51 of 206** save more or repay debt, including twenty weekly only after bills are covered.
**39 of 206** cut spending, including an eight-week pause in bowling costing 12 weekly, without cancellation fees.
**17 of 206** act with colleagues or unions, including seeking paid rosters while treating the employer’s agreement as unconfirmed.
**14 of 206** try extra income, including prepaid drawing tutorials on agreed family evenings, without upfront spending or missed paid shifts.

whatTheySay: **Useful tools** can stay without grand promises; electricians value physical repairs, clear records and enough time to finish safely.
**Paid time** and fair wages remain live issues, from union claims to requests that faster notes do not lengthen the day.
whatTheyThink: **Covered bills** and reserves make ordinary work manageable for many; practical demand and existing customers support confidence that repairs continue.
**Existing pressures** survive quieter AI: rent, paid-hour gaps, contract renewals and licence-exam failure can matter more than software.
**Room to plan** does not guarantee competence or retirement income; some keep building skills or businesses without needing a technological revolution.
howTheyFeel: **117 of 206** feel calm, generally describing covered bills, continuing work or a reserve that absorbs ordinary setbacks.
**68 are anxious** about their own or household living, while another 21 feel uneasy; none are alarmed or panicked.
**Average worry is 1.76** on the five-point scale, so little AI change coexists with substantial ordinary financial and job insecurity.

differences.text: **Worry averages 2.79** with thin cushions (72 people), versus 1.39 with moderate cushions (71) and 1.00 with strong cushions (63).
**Average worry** rises from 1.58 among early-career workers (81) to 1.84 in midlife (81) and 1.95 later (44).

least.name: Room around payday
least.story: All 117 have moderate or strong cushions; 116 carry on and 21 save more, combining a financial margin with ordinary work and plans.

most.name: Thin household margins
most.story: Of 68, 57 have thin cushions and 11 moderate; 37 cut spending while 65 carry on, showing continued work does not ensure household security.

S1.headline: Electricians test useful tools while defending paid hours around repairs that still need people.

whatTheyDo.text: **119 of 206** continue practical repairs, often keeping paper records or checking actual wages alongside existing work.
**105 of 206** choose new AI learning, such as paid trials comparing quotes or parts lists with completed repairs.
**61 of 206** act collectively, seeking written hours, paid teaching or workload agreements through unions, associations or agreed joint requests.
**45 of 206** reduce spending, cancelling optional subscriptions or postponing purchases while preserving essentials and partner agreements where specified.
**33 of 206** build savings, including thirty monthly from packed lunches only after extra food costs and essential bills.

whatTheySay: **Office tasks change first**, they say, while wiring, fault-finding and electrical checks still need real people.
**Prove the saving** with completed jobs, accurate parts and realistic travel and testing time before imposing faster schedules.
**Share the gains** through paid learning and agreed hours, including office staff and juniors rather than shifting costs onto workers.
whatTheyThink: **Work and paid hours** can shrink while repairs remain, through tighter allowances, fewer fit-outs or stronger price competition.
**Household risk** can start with a partner’s bookings, accounts or design work even while an electrician’s own repairs look secure.
**Skills and judgement** need real time; a smaller group sees more fitting work or cheaper administration for a small business.
howTheyFeel: **Anxiety leads**: 106 are anxious and three alarmed about realistic own or household income risks.
Another **eighty are uneasy** and seventeen calm; nobody is panicked.
Average **worry is 2.46**, on a scale from one for calm to five for panicked.

differences.text: Average **worry** is 2.88 for thin cushions, 2.39 for moderate cushions and 2.06 for strong cushions.
Average **worry** rises from 2.12 among early-career electricians to 2.57 in midlife and 2.89 among those later in working life.
**Collective action** appears in 54 of 69 progressive interviews, compared with four of 69 centre and three of 68 traditional interviews.
New **AI learning** appears in 61 of 69 steady interviews, 43 of 68 adaptive interviews and one of 69 resistant interviews.

S2.headline: Fast AGI makes the interval before physical robots a household income problem, with almost everyone at least anxious.

whatTheyDo.text: **105 seek support**, including available community advice, eligibility checks, family housing, childcare or help reading records.
**85 keep going**, with examples including paid repair calls, supervised shifts and finishing an existing licence.
**82 seek different work**, including posted maintenance or service jobs with workable written pay and hours.
**68 save more**, for example adding extra monthly wage deposits or repaying a van loan or mortgage.
**63 cut spending**, cancelling subscriptions, meals out or unbooked trips while replacement income remains uncertain.

whatTheySay: **The two dates** often frame public explanations: thinking tasks change first, with capable robots reaching hands-on work around 2031.
**Paid routes** feature in public demands for training, notice and worker involvement before changes to hours.
**Public reassurance** sometimes masks fear: several urge others to stay calm while privately expecting their own work to disappear.
whatTheyThink: **Household exposure** extends beyond electrical work: partners’ booking, accounts, claims and physical jobs also face cuts.
**Reserves buy room**, but many distinguish months of expenses from a lifetime wage or a guaranteed employer.
**Skills and retirement** need checking: licences cannot guarantee future work, while unverified later payments cannot fill the household budget.
howTheyFeel: **110 are alarmed** and one panicked; 94 are anxious and one uneasy, with none calm.
**Average worry is 3.54** on the five-point scale; concrete plans coexist with expected wage gaps and sleepless calculations.

differences.text: Average worry rises from **3.19** with strong cushions (63 people) to **3.46** with moderate (71) and **3.92** with thin (72).
Average worry is **3.44** among 81 younger workers, **3.53** among 81 midlife workers and **3.73** among 44 later-career workers.

S3.headline: Five years opens practical routes, but most still worry about earnings and many households lack a confirmed replacement wage.

whatTheyDo.text: **107 of 206** choose training, from inspection qualifications to practical controls classes conditional on covered fees and protected wages.
**87 of 206** continue current work, including licensed repairs and supervised junior tasks, while checking hours or household resources.
**83 of 206** save or repay debt, from meal-budget transfers to mortgage overpayments; several require essentials covered and existing reserves protected.
**63 of 206** seek different paid work; several retain current jobs until signed pay, hours and travel terms fit.
**53 of 206** seek advice, record help or household support, checking actual resources rather than assuming replacement income.

whatTheySay: **Start now** is the common public message: seek usable paid learning, clearer work terms and plans before the thinking-work change.
**Physical robots follow later**; several include office workers and partners rather than treating site workers’ preparation window as everyone’s.
**Preparation needs paid work**, with repeated requests for fees, protected weekly wages and actual tasks instead of course links.
whatTheyThink: **More time helps** some qualify, test paid routes, build businesses or strengthen reserves; others still question lasting paid demand.
**Household gaps remain** when partner desk income is exposed, current bills are tight or later physical work faces robot competition.
**Older workers need figures**, including verified retirement income and actual suitable work; birthdays and savings balances do not confirm affordable stopping.
howTheyFeel: **Anxious remains largest**: 112 of 206; 64 are uneasy, 29 alarmed and one calm; none are panicked.
**Extra warning isn’t income**: alarmed interviewees still describe expected large household losses and sleeplessness while making practical plans.
**Average worry is 2.82**, on a scale from 1 (calm) to 5 (panicked), despite practical plans for preparation.

differences.text: **Thin cushions** average 3.19 worry, versus 2.75 for moderate and 2.48 for strong cushions, on the 1–5 scale.
**Early-career workers** choose training 58/81 (72%); older workers choose support 37/44 (84%), with average worry 2.74 and 3.05 respectively.
**Steady adapters** retrain 47/69 (68%), versus 26/69 (38%) resistant and 34/68 (50%) adaptive workers; these are chosen actions, not guaranteed outcomes.

S4.headline: A decade makes preparation more manageable, but existing bills and unverified future earnings still divide electricians.

whatTheyDo.text: **116 of 206** carry on, often keeping offered paid repairs while reviewing actual hours and household costs.
**96** choose training, including practical classes only with funded costs, paid attendance and protected normal weekly wages and hours.
**69** save more or repay debt, often only from surplus after essentials while protecting existing reserves and partner agreement.
**61** seek different work, commonly requiring suitable duties and signed affordable pay and hours after travel before leaving current employment.
**53** seek help, including available advice on verified income, retirement records and eligibility without counting unapproved payments.

whatTheySay: **Ten years** should make paid practice and clear work terms possible while leaving room for ordinary family life.
Many keep **thinking AI** and later robots distinct, and resist promises that one occupation, birthday or new tool guarantees earnings.
whatTheyThink: **Current security** and later uncertainty coexist: many expect wages to continue now while still needing income after the technology dates.
**Existing bills** and possible earlier household wage cuts survive the longer warning; savings provide time, not a confirmed replacement wage.
Some see **skills, firms or assets** to build; others weigh family costs and check actual later work or retirement resources.
howTheyFeel: **31 are calm**, 87 uneasy and 88 anxious; average worry is **2.28** out of 5, with none alarmed or panicked.
Feeling **secure now** does not settle future earnings; anxiety often follows current bills, short hours or a partner's earlier thinking-work exposure.

differences.text: Mean worry: **2.85** for thin cushions (72 people), **2.13** moderate (71), **1.79** strong (63), on a five-point scale.
**36 of 44** older workers seek support, compared with 1 of 81 younger workers; older interviewees repeatedly seek verified retirement figures.
Mean worry is **2.01** among early adopters (68 people), **2.45** among steady adopters (69), and **2.36** among resistant workers (69).
